newsitem.title: USA: US official condemns logging in virgin redwood area.
newsitem.headline: US official condemns logging in virgin redwood area.

text.p: Deputy Interior Secretary John Garamendi Tuesday condemned salvage logging of the virgin All Species Grove of redwoods in Northern California, warning it could endanger an agreement to save other redwoods.
The 400-acre area is one of six virgin redwood groves at the center of a controversy that has sparked hundreds of arrests and become a focal point for environmentalists in California.
The groves are part of 200,000 acres of timberland owned by Pacific Lumber, a division of MAXXAM Inc, which faces environmental hurdles to logging because it would threaten endangered species.

A tentative agreement reached Sept. 28 between California, the federal government and the timber company set aside two virgin groves for parks, in return for $380 million in cash and land and a promise to smooth environmental problems.

Garamendi said that Charles Hurwitz, head of MAXXAM, refused to include All Species and three other virgin groves in negotiations. MAXXAM began removing dead trees Monday from All Species Grove, as they were entitled to do, he said.
"It can jeopardize the agreement," Garamendi said.
Hurwitz's action exacerbates a politically touchy situation. Environmentalists have condemned the agreement as inadequate and a "sweet deal" for Hurwitz.

Garamendi and California Democratic Sen. Dianne Feinstein, who have been on the defensive because of environmentalists' criticism since they negotiated the deal, were clearly surprised Hurwitz decided to send heavy equipment into the 2,000-year-old, untouched forest.
Garamendi said he had spoken with Hurwitz after he learned of the decision.
"He said, 'I have the right to do it.' We're not debating that," Garamendi said. "We're debating the overall effect on the public attitude."

Garamendi said it may become "impossible to gather public support to appropriate money in California or Congress to transfer land" needed for the tentative agreement, which has 10 months to become permanent.

Feinstein said she considered "salvage logging at this time counterproductive and ill-advised." Environmentalists say it can cause environmental damage, disturbing the forest floor and threatening nearby streams.
The California Board of Forestry, which has authority over the salvage logging, was to meet later in the day.
